rationale: Start with a broad organic window to locate all 10 compounds and identify the limiting separations. A 10-minute gradient at moderate temperature provides a useful scouting profile while keeping the run near the scoring time target.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve resolution without incurring a time penalty.

The limiting central pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the organic window further reduces slope, while the higher starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Narrow the gradient window again to push the sole limiting pair above R = 1.5. Raising the starting organic fraction offsets much of the slower gradient’s retention increase, targeting complete resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test whether a modest temperature increase shortens elution while preserving full resolution. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature’s effect on the limiting pair.

The limiting pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and appears to approach an elution-order crossover. Test 60 °C to move beyond that crossover and seek a faster fully resolved method, while retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test an intermediate temperature between the two high-temperature co-elution regions. At 55 °C, the central pair may remain separated after its order reversal while the earlier pair avoids its near-co-elution at 60 °C, potentially retaining CRF 1.000 with faster elution.

Slightly lengthen the 55 °C gradient to improve the pair at R = 1.41, changing only slope to measure its response. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for this adjustment while targeting full resolution before 10 minutes.

Use a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8 by lowering the endpoint to 0.80. This should preserve full resolution while bringing the last peak earlier than injection 8, maintaining the maximum CRF.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 9’s slope to seek earlier elution at the maximum CRF. This tests whether the early peaks and temperature-sensitive central pairs retain sufficient resolution at a higher starting organic fraction.

Return to the successful 40 °C selectivity and shift injection 4’s window upward without changing its slope. This tests whether all pairs remain fully resolved with earlier elution; the lower temperature should also improve retention of the early peaks relative to injection 10.

Lengthen injection 11’s gradient to recover resolution of the sole limiting pair at R = 1.20. Its last peak at 8.59 minutes leaves approximately 1.4 minutes of headroom, making full resolution before 10 minutes plausible.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to improve the early limiting pair at 55 °C, combined with a steeper gradient to shorten late elution. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved method while the maximum-score methods remain established.

Slightly steepen injection 13’s gradient by raising the endpoint, keeping its favorable starting composition and temperature. This tests whether its modest resolution margins permit faster elution while retaining CRF 1.000.

Use a gradient slope between injections 13 and 14 to target full resolution with earlier elution than injection 13. The last peak’s estimated elution composition is about 0.56, so the 0.75 endpoint should comfortably retain all peaks within the gradient.

Test whether lowering the starting organic fraction improves central selectivity enough to support a steeper, faster gradient. Injection 15 remains a maximum-score method; this run explores further shortening while monitoring both close central pairs.

Slightly reduce injection 16’s slope to improve the pair at R = 1.37 while monitoring the other close pair at R = 1.53. This targets full resolution with a last-peak time shorter than injection 15’s 7.76 minutes.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a faster gradient to seek another fully resolved region. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this run tests whether temperature-driven reordering can support shorter elution than the current 7.60-minute fully resolved method.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 °C to move the earlier close pair beyond its apparent selectivity crossover and shorten elution. This is an exploratory speed optimization; injection 17 already provides full resolution at the maximum CRF.

At 60 °C, steepening improved the limiting pair from R = 0.33 to 0.98, suggesting separation beyond an order crossover. Shorten the gradient further to test that trend, while monitoring the neighboring pair currently at R = 1.62 for compression.

Shift injection 19’s organic window downward while preserving its slope to isolate starting-composition effects on the unresolved central pair. This tests another fast selectivity region without sacrificing the established maximum-score methods.

Test the previously unexplored 50 °C selectivity at the same gradient as injection 21. This isolates temperature’s effect and checks whether an intermediate-temperature elution order can provide full resolution in a substantially shorter run.

Test 35 °C with an intermediate gradient slope to explore selectivity between the crowded 30 °C profile and the successful 40 °C methods. This may separate the central cluster while keeping the last peak earlier than the established 40 °C fully resolved runs.

Trim injection 17’s gradient endpoint and duration while preserving its slope and temperature. The estimated last-peak elution composition is 0.57, below the new endpoint, so this shorter programmed gradient should preserve its fully resolved, maximum-score chromatogram.

Preserve injection 13’s successful slope and temperature while trimming the programmed gradient to 8 minutes. Its last peak’s estimated elution composition is 0.56, below the new endpoint, so this should retain CRF 1.000 with slightly larger resolution margins than injection 24.
